agriculture

/AG-rih-kuhl-cher/ - the stress falls on AG · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Agriculture means the practice of farming, including growing crops and raising livestock.

The valley's economy rests on agriculture: apples on the slopes, dairy herds on the flats, and a seed company in town.

Example

The museum's timeline of human invention gives one wall to fire, one to the wheel, and three to a handful of seeds — the birth of agriculture. Around ten thousand years ago, people in a crescent of hills stopped only gathering wild grain and began planting it, keeping the plumpest heads to sow again, penning the tamest goats instead of chasing wild ones. Cities, writing, and kings all queue up behind that wall — none of them happens without it.

Agriculture is the exact word for what began there: the practice of farming, including growing crops and raising livestock. It is wider than any one farm or harvest — the whole age-old project of raising food on purpose rather than finding it, from rice paddies to sheep stations to the science of soil itself.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

husbandry: Husbandry is the careful tending of what you already raise, especially animals — feeding, breeding, keeping stock healthy. Agriculture is the whole enterprise around it, crops and livestock together; husbandry is one skill inside agriculture, not the name of the entire field.

cultivation: Cultivation is the tending side of growing — preparing soil, planting, and coaxing crops along. It stops at plants; agriculture takes in livestock too, naming the whole practice and industry of raising food, in the field and in the barn alike.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

wilderness: land left entirely unfarmed and untended

industry: making goods in factories rather than raising food from the ground

Where it sits · the scale of food production — gardening → farming → agriculture

gardening vs. agriculture: Gardening sits at the small end of this scale, feeding one household bed by bed and mostly for the love of it, while agriculture spans everything people do to raise food, from paddies to dairy barns.

farming vs. agriculture: Farming goes further than gardening — one family's land and livelihood; agriculture claims the widest ground of all, every farm, flock, and grain silo counted together as one practice.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — agri-

Root — agri-: field (Latin ager)

Root — cult-

Root — cult-: to till, to tend

Suffix — -ure

Suffix — -ure: activity, result

Put it together

Put it together: Agri- (field) + cult- (to till, to tend) + -ure (activity) = the activity of tending the fields. Latin agricultura says it plainly: field-tending. Ten thousand years of it separate the wild grass from the loaf of bread.

Use the root in a new word: horticulture

Use the root in a new word: horticulture: After two summers on a landscaping crew, she enrolled in a horticulture program.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / academic

Agriculture is the umbrella word — ministries, textbooks, and census forms use it to cover crops and livestock together. When you mean one person's work or one piece of land, farming is the natural word. Keep it apart from this unit's agrarian, which describes societies and eras: agriculture is what farmers do; agrarian is what a whole world built on farming is.
